steps.prompt: Two dice are rolled and added. There are $11$ possible sums, from $2$ to $12$. Is the chance of a sum of $7$ equal to $\frac{1}{11}$? Why or why not?

cards.title: Good over all
cards.body: When all outcomes are equally likely, $P(\text{event}) = \frac{\text{good outcomes}}{\text{all outcomes}}$. Probability is counting twice. Make the outcomes equally likely first: for two dice, list $36$ ordered pairs, not $11$ sums.

cards.title: Worked example: a sum of 8
cards.problem: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is $8$?

try.prompt: How many of the $36$ pairs give a sum of $8$?
What is the probability, as a fraction?

cards.title: Opposites and "and"
cards.body: $P(\text{not } E) = 1 - P(E)$, which is great for "at least one". For independent events, $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)$. Drawing without putting back changes the second draw: count with $\binom{n}{k}$ or multiply fractions that shrink.

cards.title: Worked example: two from a bag
cards.problem: A bag holds $3$ red and $5$ blue marbles. Two are taken out at once. What is the probability that both are red?

steps.text: $\binom{3}{2} = 3$ pairs are both red, so the probability is $\frac{3}{28}$. (Check: $\frac{3}{8} \times \frac{2}{7} = \frac{3}{28}$.)

try.prompt: What is the probability that both are red?

cards.title: The common trap: outcomes that aren't equally likely
cards.body: The $11$ dice sums, or the $4$ possible numbers of heads in $3$ flips, are not equally likely. Count the basic outcomes instead. And watch for replacement: without it, the second draw has one fewer marble.

prompts: How do you make sure the outcomes you count are equally likely?
